title: Sugared almonds
subtitle: whole almonds panned in a sugar syrup shell with a crisp, opaque coating
excerpt: Sugared almonds are whole roasted almonds cooked in a sugar syrup on the hob until the syrup dries and crystallises around each nut in a thick, white coating. The coating is applied in several stages, with the syrup added in small amounts and stirred continuously between additions. The finished almonds are light, crisp, and sweet.
sourceNotes: Sugar-coated almonds (dragees) have been made in France since at least the sixteenth century. They were traditionally given as wedding favours and to mark christenings. The French town of Verdun has produced dragees since the thirteenth century and remains closely associated with them.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 weeks.

content.text: Sugared almonds are whole almonds coated in a thick, white sugar shell by cooking them repeatedly in sugar syrup on the hob. Each batch of syrup is added small, stirred in until it evaporates, and allowed to crystallise around the nuts before the next addition goes in. The process takes around 30 minutes of steady stirring but produces consistently even, opaque-coated almonds.
Spread the almonds on a baking tray and roast at 180 degrees C (fan 160 degrees C) for 8 minutes until lightly golden. Let cool slightly.
Put the sugar and water in a medium heavy-based saucepan. Stir over low heat until the sugar dissolves, then bring to the boil without stirring. Add the almonds and vanilla if using.

Stir continuously over medium heat. The syrup will cook down and eventually begin to crystallise and coat the nuts in a white, sandy layer. This is the first coating. Continue stirring as the sugar melts again into a second syrup around the now-coated nuts.

The coating-and-remelting cycle repeats naturally as you stir. After about 20 to 25 minutes, the coating will be thick, white, and opaque. The almonds will clump together at first but separate as the coating builds.
Tip onto a baking paper-lined tray while hot and use two forks to separate any almonds that are stuck together. Leave to cool completely. The coating will harden as it cools.

attrs.problem: Sugar crystallising unevenly with clumps of white powder not sticking
attrs.avoid: Avoid reducing the heat too quickly; the syrup needs consistent medium heat to crystallise evenly.
attrs.fix: Keep stirring and maintain medium heat. The sandy, uneven phase is normal and resolves as you continue stirring and the sugar remelts.

attrs.problem: Almonds sticking together in large clumps
attrs.avoid: Avoid leaving the pan unattended; clumps form when the nuts sit together in pooled syrup.
attrs.fix: Stir constantly and separate clumps with the spoon as you go. Once on the tray, use two forks to pull them apart before the coating sets hard.
